# What is an oil catch can for?

An oil catch can serves a specific mechanical function: it intercepts crankcase ventilation gases before they re-enter the intake manifold. To understand why this matters, we must look at the physics of internal combustion and how modern engines manage pressure and temperature. Every time your engine burns fuel, some liquid fuel and oil inevitably leak past the piston rings into the crankcase rather than being fully combusted. This mixture creates a pressurized environment known as crankcase pressure.

Modern engines utilize a Positive Crankcase Ventilation (PCV) system to manage this pressure. The PCV valve acts as a one-way check valve, drawing these vapors out of the crankcase and routing them back into the intake stream to be burned off in the combustion chamber. This is an efficient way to prevent oil leaks and maintain structural integrity, but it introduces a critical flaw: the gas stream carries suspended oil mist with it.

Without intervention, this mist travels through the intake manifold and settles on the intake valves and cylinder walls. Over time, this leads to carbon buildup, reduced compression, and eventually, rough idling or loss of power. An oil catch can addresses this by acting as a simple but effective separator. Typically installed inline between the crankcase (via the PCV valve) and the intake manifold, the device forces the gas stream through a filter media or into a chamber where velocity drops significantly.

The mechanism relies on gravity and inertia. As the high-velocity vapor hits the baffle plates or the filter element inside the canister, the heavier oil droplets lose momentum and settle to the bottom of the reservoir. The cleaner gas then passes through a vent at the top of the catch can and continues into the intake system. This prevents the direct deposition of fresh oil mist onto your cold intake valves.

It is crucial to distinguish what an oil catch can actually solves versus common misconceptions found in enthusiast forums. The source material notes that RX-8 owners recommend these devices to prevent problems from "overfilling" the oil. If we interpret this literally, one might assume the catch can reduces the total volume of liquid oil inside the engine block. That is not how the physics works. An oil catch can does not reduce the quanity of oil in your sump; it only captures the mist that has already been thrown up from the oil level.

Therefore, installing a catch can will not alleviate the risks associated with mechanically overfilling the engine, such as foaming oil or hydro-locking, which are detailed in technical discussions regarding excessive lubricant levels. If you add too much oil via your dipstick, the excess liquid remains in the crankcase regardless of what is happening upstream. The catch can merely stops the *mist* generated by that agitation from coating your intake ports.

From a maintenance perspective, the trade-off involves the lifecycle of the filter itself. Because the device captures particulate matter and condensed oil, the internal media will eventually become saturated. Unlike a standard air filter that is replaced less frequently, the catch can filter requires periodic inspection or replacement. Neglecting this maintenance defeats the purpose of the installation, as a clogged restrictor can actually hinder the flow of crankcase gases, potentially leading to increased blow-by and higher oil consumption over the long term.

If you are maintaining an older air-cooled engine or a rotary powerplant like the Renesis, the necessity of this component becomes more pronounced due to the higher operating temperatures and different sealing characteristics of those specific architectures. For modern water-cooled engines with direct injection, valve coating is less of a concern because fuel injectors spray directly into the cylinder, bypassing the intake valves. However, for port-injected engines, an oil catch can remains a valid strategy to extend the interval between cleaning sessions and maintain peak volumetric efficiency.

When sourcing parts for such modifications, ensure you select a unit compatible with your specific PCV routing. Some systems use a T-fitting that allows flow in both directions depending on engine speed, while others rely on a specific check valve configuration. Always verify the fitment before purchasing to avoid leaks that could lead to vacuum leaks or unfiltered air ingestion.
